1:
Everything here turns on who the king is, and the answers are not compatible. Clarke states his flatly: it is "a nuptial song, which primarily respected Solomon's marriage with the daughter of Pharaoh", with "a prophetic reference to the conversion of the Gentiles" laid over it. Calvin agrees it was "composed concerning Solomon", but holds that "whatever excellence had been seen in Solomon had a higher application", the union of Christ and his Church being set forth under a type. Delitzsch reports the older claim: the Epistle to the Hebrews "proceeds on the assumption that it is the future Christ", and the Targum already renders the second verse "Thy beauty, O King Messiah", so "this Messianic interpretation must be very ancient." Gill and Spurgeon address Christ throughout. Wesley argues from fit: the praise is "most true of Christ; but not of Solomon; whom many have excelled".

Clarke, having named Solomon, then concedes the point verse by verse. Of the everlasting blessing: "This, I am afraid, could in no sense be ever spoken of Solomon; but of the man Christ Jesus it is strictly true." Of the girded sword: "He was not a warlike prince." Of the riding: "They are true only of Christ."

The title divides them too. Henry offers both readings of its first word — an instrument of six strings, or the lilies "strewed, with other flowers, at nuptial solemnities" — and takes the flowers for Christ. Clarke will have none of it: "a world of labor has been spent to prove that these lilies mean the saints", and "I cannot believe that any such meaning is intended." He takes the versions' "for those who shall be changed" for the calling of the Gentiles. Augustine builds a sermon on that same phrase: the world is what was changed, "lately worshipping idols, now worshipping God" — and each believer likewise, "from an infidel to a believer: from a thief to a giver of alms".

"Inditing" satisfies nobody. Ellicott calls it "a most unhappy rendering" of a word whose derivative means a pot or cauldron, so that it must mean "to boil over" or "to bubble up". Spurgeon hears the heat: the stanzas are "the natural outburst of his soul", and "heartless hymns are insults to heaven." Ellicott also corrects the article: "my poem is of a king (not the king)". Wesley reduces the poet to "the pen".

On the king's beauty the Hebrew is emphatic. Spurgeon notes the doubled word — "Beautiful, beautiful art thou" — and Ellicott renders "Fair art thou; aye, fairer than". Gill limits the claim: not divine beauty, "for this admits of no comparison", but the beauty of the human nature. Ellicott finds the "flowing grace" on the lips ambiguous between "the beauty of the mouth" and "the charm of its speech", and treats the misplaced "therefore" as a refrain, the poet "interrupted by the acclaim of his hearers" — hearers whom Clarke identifies as the bride's companions, speaking the psalm after its first verse.

The warrior verses are read as ideal, not ceremonial. Ellicott prefers "gird on thy hero's sword", takes the glory and majesty in apposition to it — "his weapon was the monarch's glory and pride" — and dismisses any allusion to an enthronement custom, since "the next verse shows that we have rather an ideal picture". Gill makes the sword "the word of God... a twoedged one, consisting of law and Gospel"; Spurgeon prays it out of storage: "Why should the sword of the Spirit lie still, like a weapon hung up in an armoury?" Ellicott rearranges the fifth verse as the poet saw it — "Thine arrows are sharpened— The people under Thee fall— Against the heart of the king's enemies" — while Clarke reads the arrows as convictions, under which "those who received the word rose again by repentance and faith; those who did not, fell down."
6:
"Thy throne, O God" is the verse the chapter is fought over, and Ellicott will not take it as it stands. The received rendering is the ancient versions', but whether they meant it of God or of the theocratic king "is uncertain", and the Christian application "does not help us to explain how the monarch, who is the poet's theme here, could be addressed as God" — the more so in an Elohistic psalm, where the usual parallels do not satisfy him. He proposes two alternatives: "thy divine throne", or "Thy throne is of God for ever", which he calls "grammatically preferable".

Gill anticipates those readings and forbids them: the words "will not bear to be rendered, 'thy throne is the throne of God', or 'thy throne is God'; or be supplied thus, 'God shall establish thy throne'." Clarke argues from the apostle who quoted it: "if the apostle did not believe Jesus Christ to be the true and eternal God, he has utterly misapplied this Scripture." Against the version "God is thy throne" he answers that "the nominative case is often used for the vocative, particularly by the Attics, and the whole scope of the place requires it should be so used here." Wesley argues from continuity: the address has not changed hands since the first verse, and the same person is called king and God, "to assure us that he doth not speak of Solomon". Henry assigns the speech — "it is God the Father that says to the Son here" — and reads the sceptre's rightness as exactness, the administration being "exactly according to the eternal counsel and will of God".

The anointing turns the psalm from war to wedding. Clarke reads the oil as evidence "that all causes of mourning, sorrow, and death, were at an end", since in mourning "the ancients did not anoint themselves." Ellicott places it in the ceremony, since the bath and anointing "formed part of the Oriental marriage proceedings", and takes the "fellows" for "the paranymphs, or attendants on the bridegroom"; Wesley takes them for another company altogether, "all that ever were anointed for priests or prophets, or kings". Delitzsch marks the structural turn: the song "has portrayed the lovely king as a man, as a hero, and as a divine ruler; now it describes him as a bridegroom" — a sequence he reads as the history of the future, the avenging victories preparing the way for "the marriage of the Lamb".

On the perfumed garments Clarke is the ethnographer: "the Asiatics are very partial to perfumes", and the ivory palaces are not palaces but "the wardrobes inlaid with ivory, in which their numerous changes of raiment were deposited". Ellicott would rather carry the anointing forward from the previous verse: the garments "are anointed with" the spices, which "may have been ingredients of the oil of gladness". Wesley allows the ivory palaces to be the heavenly mansions, but adds the caution the whole psalm needs: "there is no necessity to strain every particular circumstance in such poetical descriptions."

The women of the ninth verse divide the literal from the ecclesiastical. Clarke finds no difficulty on the historical reading — "we know he had seven hundred wives, princesses" — while on the other it means the gospel reaching "many of the kings, queens, and nobles, of the earth". Ellicott stays with the court: the honourable women are literally "precious ones, i.e., possibly the favourites of the harem", the queen "was stationed" rather than stood, "referring to the position assigned to the bride when the marriage procession was formed". Wesley makes the queen the church and the attendants individual believers, conceding that though the church "is made up of particular believers, yet she is distinguished from them, for the decency of the parable". Delitzsch, turning to the bride, puts himself in the place of one "who addresses the bridal pair at the altar".
10:
Who is speaking to the bride is unsettled, and Gill declines to settle it: the words are "either spoken by the prophet, the author of the psalm; or by the King, the bridegroom himself; or, as others think, by Jehovah the Father", unless they are the address of "the honourable women" to their mistress. Clarke takes the last — the companions, having described the bridegroom, now turn to her. Wesley takes the first, and hears the tone: the poet "speaks like an elder person, and as her spiritual father and counsellor", using several words for one thing "to shew his vehement desire of her good". Henry takes the second: "God, who said to the Son, Thy throne is for ever and ever, says this to the church."

Henry reads the three verbs as a sequence and a rule of reading in general: "he that has ears, let him hearken diligently; he that hearkens, let him consider and weigh it duly; he that considers, let him incline and yield to the force of what is laid before him." Spurgeon takes the third literally: "lean forward that no syllable may be unheard."

The forgetting is the hard command, and every voice qualifies it. Wesley disposes of it in a word: "comparatively". Henry likewise makes it proportion, to love family "less than Christ", but presses the historical edge: converts "from Judaism or paganism to the faith of Christ" must "wholly cast out the old leaven", bringing along neither the Jewish ceremonies nor the heathen idolatries, "for these would make such a mongrel religion in Christianity as the Samaritans had". His warning against looking back is drawn from Lot's wife. Spurgeon guards the same limit from the other side — "not that natural ties are broken by grace, but ties of the sinful nature" — then removes the temptation altogether: "why should we remember the Egypt from which we came out? Are the leeks and the garlic, and the onions anything, when the iron bondage, and the death-dealing Pharaoh of hell are remembered?"

Clarke supplies the historical scene and its transfer in a stroke. To the Egyptian princess the sense is: "Thou art now become the spouse of the most magnificent monarch in the universe. Forget therefore thy own people — the Egyptians, and take the Israelites in their place." Taken of Christ, the same words become "an address to the Gentiles to forsake their idolatrous customs". Henry supplies the incentive: mixing the old rites into her religion "would blemish her beauty and would hazard her interest in the affections of the royal bridegroom".

The beauty desired is described as borrowed rather than owned. Gill insists it "is not natural, nor acquired by her, but what is given her", being "perfect through the comeliness of her Lord upon her". Ellicott gives only the gesture: worship means "literally, bow down or prostrate thyself". Delitzsch warns against reading the scene as one occasion, since the poet "combines on the canvas of one picture things that lie wide apart both as to time and place", seeing the bride first in her own chamber.

Tyre is read as a sample rather than a subject. Ellicott rearranges the clauses — "The Tyrians with a gift entreat thy favour, The rich ones of the people" — and answers the objection that Tyre was never subject to Israel: "the gifts may be complimentary presents", not tribute. He also unpacks the idiom of entreating, "literally, stroke thy face", though since the root idea is polishing, one might render "makes thy face bright or joyful". Clarke makes the city stand for a maritime world: as "the greatest maritime and commercial city in the world", it represents the coasts "which first received the Gospel of Christ". Wesley agrees, Tyre being "the mart of the nations"; Gill reads a prophecy of the Tyrians' conversion, fulfilled "in the times of Christ and his apostles".
13:
"All glorious within" is where the literal and the devotional readings meet head-on. Ellicott dismisses one outright: the phrase means "in the interior, in the inner room of the palace", and "the next clause would alone dismiss the reference to moral qualities from which has sprung such a wealth of mystic interpretation." He then asks which palace, and answers that it cannot be the bridegroom's, "since the procession has not yet reached its destination"; she waits "in her own apartments". Clarke reaches the same literal sense by custom rather than syntax: the Asiatic queens "scarcely ever appear in public", abiding in the harem "in the greatest luxury and splendor".

Spurgeon takes precisely the reading Ellicott has ruled out: the passage "may be understood as meaning within herself — her beauty is not outward only or mainly; the choicest of her charms are to be found in her heart, her secret character", since "mere skin-deep beauty is nothing in his eyes." Gill keeps both senses side by side, within doors in the inner chamber and within the hearts of her members.

The clothing is corrected on the same principle. Ellicott makes wrought gold "textures woven with gold" and recalls "the custom of repeatedly changing the bride's dress during the marriage ceremonies, every time presenting her in greater magnificence than before". On the raiment of needlework he removes the garment altogether: "this is now more generally understood of rich tapestry carpets spread for the procession." Clarke describes the enclosed litter in which "no part of her person is visible"; Wesley notes the custom "of conducting the bride to the bridegroom's house."

At the sixteenth verse the address changes hands, and Wesley argues it from grammar: the speech returns to the bridegroom, "as may be gathered from the Hebrew words, which are of the masculine gender". He turns that into an argument against Solomon, whose children "were so far from being made Princes in all the earth, that they enjoyed but a small part of their father's dominions." Clarke, who reads the verse as spoken to the bride — "instead of the kindred, which thou hast left behind in Egypt, thou shalt have numerous children" — concedes the same point: it "cannot refer either to Solomon, or to the daughter of Pharaoh; for there is no evidence that he ever had a child by Pharaoh's daughter", nor was his successor her son. Gill takes the children for the apostles and then "a numerous progeny among the Gentiles".

Delitzsch refuses to choose. The promise "has its first and most natural meaning in relation to contemporary history but without being at variance with the reference of the Psalm to the King Messiah": as the kings of Judah and Israel let their sons share the dominion, so from this union "there spring up children, to whom the regal glory of the house of David which culminates in Him is transferred." Ellicott finds historical illustrations in a king's son governing a city, and in the realm divided into principalities. Spurgeon reads the succession as continuous rather than dynastic: "the veterans depart, but volunteers fill up the vacant places. The line of grace never becomes extinct."

The closing promise is taken by three of them as fulfilled in the psalm itself. Gill says the psalmist made the name remembered "by penning of this psalm, which has been the occasion of the remembrance of Christ's name in all ages". Clarke says it more sharply: "the constant use of this Psalm in the Christian Church is a literal fulfillment of the prophecy." Wesley notes only that the song "should not only serve for the present solemnity, but should be remembered and sung in all successive generations". Spurgeon adds the contrast that gives it force: "names renowned in one generation have been unknown to the next era, but the laurels of Jesus shall ever be fresh."
